Max is a decent professor. His lectures were mainly discussing content and then doing lots of practice problems. Discrete math can be somewhat hard to teach as sometimes as a student you just have to get it. So honestly, he did a pretty good job at teaching content. My main complaint was the lack of consistency with grading and feedback from the TA's. The head TA Josh was very good, however. So ultimately, Max is a good professor. Just be prepared for some bumps in the road, but in the end, it'll all work out.

He's a funny and interesting lecturer, but also an extremely disorganized one. Many lecturers often are rushed through because he goes off on tangents, which, while interesting, they lead to speeding through challenging content. He also takes a long time to respond to emails and comes off as condescending. Exams are very challenging for two reasons: 1. They can be difficult to prepare for. Since there are extremely abstract questions, you likely have never seen them before. Practice exams do not fully reflect what will be on the actual exam. They are sometimes unavailable and answer keys have incorrect/unclear answers. 2. Questions often contain ambiguous language, making it difficult to understand what exactly is being asked. On one exam, a question was written so poorly that nobody in the class correctly answered it. Overall, I would avoid taking this class with Max unless you absolutely need it. Save yourself the trouble and take it with Fardina.

Cliff is very hard to reach at times when you are trying to schedule office hours, barely interacts with the class during his lectures and worst of all he does not curve. If you take him, I recommend doing your best to get the percentage of the grade you want because he will not help you curve to the next letter grade. You're basically on your own. The quizzes were questionable in terms of difficulty, and his lectures barely covered them.

Nelson is the chillest professor. He understands students needs and teaches important material. This class was very easy though. Projects are mostly changing things from the examples he has in class. The tests are a lot of info to memorize but I found that it wasn't graded so harshly.

I don't think Ting's lectures are as bad as people made them out to be but her biggest problem was that she sometimes made difficult concepts more complicated to learn. So the best thing you can do is briefly read Justin's notes before going to her lecture, because she will on occasion, give hints on exams Her exams are very fair, and there are no curveballs (higher averages than Justin's) And she's very helpful in office hours if you need help whether it's lecture material or exams Oh yeah she has snacks in office hours and you're free to take some Overall I think she's fine and it's just her 2nd semester I'm sure she'll improve later on

This semester we had 6 "short" exams that ranged from 12-22 pages long each. Class materials were given to us via youtube links. She also was too lazy to fix mistakes in the exams and material she gave us. Overall, not too hard to get a good grade, but the tests do take a considerable amount of time.

Yo please do not take this prof, she is so unorganized and she is so bad at teaching. During lectures she contradicts herself each time when a student asks a question. She also makes the exams look nothing like the practice that she gives. To add on, when she answers questions, she is always not sure about her answer. The grading in this class is so bad that they release grades two months after the deadline. PLEASE AVOID THIS PROF
You are expected to put in an exceptional amount of effort. DO NOT take with any other hard classes

He is a great and nice guy, but it seems his greatest flaw is being too smart since he administers challenging weekly homework, fast-paced 15-minute weekly quizzes, and 4 hellish projects throughout the semester. The grade cutoffs are shifted dramatically to compensate for this wild difficulty. If you ever need a deadline extended or to redo a quiz, he will work with you: indeed, he cares about his students and their learning in this class. He posts all of his slideshows, is good at responding to emails, often has online Zoom lectures, and will be sometimes lenient on grading quizzes. If I were to take the class again, I would not take Nari but this is only because the other options—usually Justin—are just superb teachers too.

Terrible professor. Do not take him. Had him for CMSC 250 and CMSC 421 (summer). The class was entirely online with the exception of exams. He was not punctual with lecture postings, rarely responded to students on piazza, and if he did respond, it would be one word answers. He did not show up to either the midterm or final. Exams were terribly worded.

Marine is a very knowledgeable professor who explains topics well and can answer questions during class extremely well. She is understanding and accommodating while not being a pushover. The class is organized well and homework and exams are fair. I definitely recommend Marine.

Sigh.... Where do I even begin? This class has been the biggest pain in my side all semester, and may be the reason why I need to take an extra semester to graduate. Professor Abadi himself isn't a bad guy at all-- he's kind and understanding, and his lectures aren't that bad, but all those things mean nothing if he plans on purposely giving students constant stress and headaches with his class. Here's a list of reasons why I personally hated every second of being in this class (and why you may as well): - He assigns textbook readings to learn class content before he teaches it in lecture. I have never once agreed that this is a good way to teach any course, ever. - He assigns reading quizzes before class and lecture quizzes during class, both of which are graded for ACCURACY. So essentially if you found anything in the textbook confusing on any given night you can forget about getting your participation points that day. - His projects are wayyyyyyyyy too complicated. The first project on basic queries should have been clear and straightforward, since we were only about 2 weeks into SQL at that point, yet all of the queries were something the lines of: "create a query to find passengers between the ages of 16 to 44 who took flights with American Airlines in January or Delta in May where the passengers also flew with at least 3 other passenger above the age of 60 that normally fly with an airline other than Delta or American" (students will vouch that this isn't much of an exaggeration). Don't get me started on the B+ tree project, it was easily the most unnecessary information overload I've ever had to deal with. If I ever want to feel the feeling of being completely and utterly overwhelmed again, I'm just gonna read over that project again. - He purposely makes his tests hard (and tells you). He claims it's because he cares about you and that there will be a curve and that we shouldn't worry about our grades too much, so I walked out of our midterm thinking I got a B+ after a decent attempt and ended up getting a 63 after a 15 point curve. He also claimed that he tried to design it to give as much partial credit as possible, but I got all 0's on a series of 8 short answer questions that didn't even have options for partial credit. - He doesn't post announcements on ELMS for critical information, nor basically anywhere for that matter. He has a piazza, but not often will you find a helpful disclaimer or reminder that is clearly marked. Don't take this course with Abadi, and if you do, you better hope you aren't signed up for any other difficult courses, or you will be pulling hairs out of your head all semester.

He speeds through content, only cares to explain the technicals and math and not general concepts that would make the math easier to absorb, and lecture structure is confusing and often logically backwards, likely because he splices slide decks together from other classes he's taught. It makes easy content difficult to grasp, and it makes difficult content impossible to even get started with. And there's no book accompanying this course, so you're stuck with his scattered, lightning fast lectures, whatever you can find on Youtube, and absolutely no practice (I mean it -- none) with the content on exams. His high score is absolutely undeserved (and baffling to me). I feel like I know less now than I did walking into the class.

Jose has incredible passion for teaching and really cares about his students, and the lectures reflect that. Definitely take Jose if you have the chance for any class — you'll learn a ton and enjoy the course

Reviews saying he grades on his opinion are pretty spot on. Gets decently rude in comments on the term project, but grades light(ish). Exams are very easy, and course is overall light except craming the coding portion of the project in mid semester. Can be frustrating though.

Marsh taught the iOS version of this class when I took it and I also took 420 with him the previous semester. Class is structured like Marsh's other classes: - Projects are the majority of your grade in this class - There are exams but they are online on gradescope, open note, open internet - Class is flipped model, so lectures are prerecorded and you are expected to watch them before class. During actual lecture time, he goes over examples which may or may not be helpful. The projects outside of the first one are graded by hand by TAs and they are pretty lenient with grading. Be fully prepared to teach yourself for this class and pray you get good TAs the semester you take it. There will be a group project to design an app, which is very open ended. My biggest complaint is with the final project. It felt very cobbled together and it was released far too late into the semester, while we had other projects to do as well. Overall, Marsh is one of the nicest, most accommodating professors in the department, but takes a while to get used to. His lectures can be very boring and 436 itself seemed to fall apart organizationally towards the end of the semester.

Laxman has been my favorite professor so far in my career at UMD. He has a strong passion for the course material and is always looking for ways to make the course more effective in passing that passion on to students. In many ways, 451 just picks up where 351 finished, so you spend time diving deep into a lot of different algorithmic ideas and patterns in a way that really helps you to strengthen your algorithmic thinking. It's also still just a survey course of algorithms, and after finishing this course I feel like a whole world has opened up to me. This semester we had competitive programming-style homework problems on CodeForces as well as written theory homeworks. You could pick any language you liked to implement your solutions. I really liked this way of teaching the course since it kept a strong focus on algorithm theory (very fun) but also forces you to really understand how to implement algorithms in practice. Definitely take Laxman, he cares.

Anybody but this guy especially if its CMSC456, just wait another semester until an actual good prof is scheduled to teach this class. I came in excited to learn about Cryptography and I'm leaving hoping that I never have to do any Cryptography for the rest of my life

Fun coding course where I learned some pretty interesting concepts compared to other theory heavy coding classes. Be good student, don't be lazy, show up on time, and study and you are guaranteed at least a B.

Prof. Wilson is a very passionate and understanding instructor. Although it is sometimes difficult to follow his lectures because he talks a lot about how specific equations are derived or the theoretical concept at the core of the lesson, he does lots of practice problems and posts extra if we run out of time during the class. You can clearly feel his passion for teaching and the class; he makes the lectures engaging and he always stays after class to answer questions from students. In terms of grading, the partial credit was very generous for most of the midterms, and there was even an opportunity for point recovery on one. The midterms were reflective of the practice tests he posted beforehand. The only criticism I would have are that the online H.W. questions were often not representative of what we covered in class and were unnecessarily hard. For studying for tests, the worksheets handed out during discussions were a much better resource than the H.W. But overall, I recommend Prof. Wilson if you're taking MATH140 as he clearly cares about his students and has reasonable expectations and exams.

Dr Williams was honestly a great professor. He is always open to answering questions and his test are very fair if you do his suggested problems and hw, sometimes they are even the same questions. The final was decently harder than the rest of his test but thats to be expected. If you have the opportunity to take Dr. Williams definitely do so. He also doesn’t do minuses which is nice for GPA.

Professor Song is really nice. However, she doesn't teach the material very well, and it's hard to follow her notes. Yet, her quizzes are free points, and her tests are easy and similar to her practice tests. TA discussions are very helpful, most of the time I learned the material better from them. 3.5 stars.

Absolutely amazing professor. I will say, he is one of the top 3 professors I have ever taken when it comes to Math, he is so patient and explains everything in such a clear and simple way. I rarely recall him ever going through the theoretical versions of what he was teaching because he realized most of the class were engineering majors who wouldn't really use such theory, and tried to incorporate a more application-oriented reasoning, while also not getting too carried away with it. I really recommend him for Calc 3, and probably any math course. I will most definitely be on the lookout for him when I decide to take Linear Algebra. The only con is that he goes pretty fast when it comes to lectures, but he won't turn you down if you need him to go over something again.

I don't get all the Doucette hate. This was her second semester ever teaching and she was tasked with teaching the juggernaut of diffeq. The only critique I have of her is that sometimes she can go a little fast during lecture and can get sidetracked because of a question someone asks. She is not a bad professor and was much better than Stefan. Her exams are fair and she will not be the reason you do bad. She provides so many resources and opportunities for you to learn the material so you don't bomb a midterm. She is lenient with grading and the final isn't worth 50%, which is what the final was worth if you took Stefan. She used to lecture on the chalkboard but in the middle of the semester, she switched to lecturing on pen and paper and projected them on the projector and then scanned the notes and posted them on canvas. Overall, she is a good professor and her exams are fair, I would take her again.

Dr. G is the best 310 professor without a doubt. He is an amazing and caring professor who wants everyone to succeed in his class and in future classes. His exams were fair and the quizzes and homework helped a ton. Part of what makes him a great professor is he has a PhD in Math Education, so he understands the concepts very well and understands how to teach students. My only complaint is I cannot take him for every class.

Like the other review said, he doesn’t teach applications. The class feels like 240 all over again and the homework is busy work. He doesn’t use the same textbook as Justin so Justin’s notes won’t help you and the final is worth 40% of our grade. Felt like I wasted a semester taking 401 with him
He is an awesome teacher! I really enjoyed his lectures. I definitely didn't find the class easy but the exams and quizzes were fair.

This course is pretty tough (I mean it's a 400-level), though the assignments are not too hard. I honestly wanted more homework because I didn't feel prepared for the exam, but it was fine. This was my first 400-level math class (taken concurrently with 406), and it definitely took some effort. The textbook is pretty poorly written and unhelpful, but you can find free textbooks for proof-based linear algebra online. If you have already taken 403, I imagine this class is significantly nicer just because the notation learning curve is steep. Adam is pretty responsive to student feedback. You just have to speak up.
On one end, he's a great lecturer, curves pretty substantially, and administers fair exams. That being said, he doesn't post notes, and homework are quite lengthy, and are graded very stringently.

Second everything said in previous reviews. Dr. Nguyen is the best math professor I have had at UMD and one of the best professors I've had at UMD period. He clearly communicated expectations and lecture material and also had a subtle sense of humor I really liked. Like others mentioned, the homeworks were tough but fair and his office hours were extremely helpful. Would take another one of his classes in a heartbeat.

Dr. Nguyen is a great professor! I had him for both MATH410 and 411, which are important classes for going into higher level math, and his lectures are organized, and he involves the class as well. There's also enough humor to make it somewhat fun while still keeping it as professional as it needs to be. The homework assignments are difficult but reasonable, and he is great at helping if you're having any problems with the hw in office hours. The exams are also reasonable. I would 100% recommend taking 410/411 with him

Dr. Buehrle is a good professor but the lectures can get boring and luckily he records them so you don't have to go in-person. XTA HW can be quite tricky with some explanations making no sense or us never really learning the concept. 3 Lecture exams, with the lowest being dropped, were quite difficult...but heavily curved. The only bad thing I can say is that the TAs were soooooo slow at grading lab reports and sometimes grading exams (one even grades in pencil...like wtf?). Anyways overall, chill professor and would recommend to anyone.

He is a great guy. He curves a LOT and he knows everyone is just taking physics for the requirement and that none of us are interested in. He knows a lot more about physics than you need for this class which can be helpful BUT he doesn't teach what will be graded. He teaches convoluted and theoretical physics and then everyone bombs the exams. He then curves each individual exam by a lot so everyone ends up with decent grades. He is funny and a good lecturer but the curriculum is just terrible and lab is the worst part of the class.

Dr.Severson is a great professor. His teaching style isn't the best but he still manages to explain things clear enough. There are some instances were he would get confused since he is using another professor's teaching material. My biggest concern with his class was that since it was online when I took it, there were a lot of people cheating on his exams and it showed on the averages. We had 2 midterms and the average on each of them was ~80% which is very high considering the difficulty of the exams. While this was not entirely Dr. Severson's fault, this could have been prevented if he had muted the exams after it was completed. When I took the class, he had it where you had the whole weekend to take the exam with about 75 minutes to complete it once you start it. When you finished the exam, it would tell you what you got wrong and the correct answers to the questions. This allowed some people in our class to cheat artificially raising the average and almost lowering the curve/cutoff.

Really good professor who is really passionate about the content she teaches. Very good at answering questions and she offers a retake midterm which she'll average with the original midterm. Her voice doesn't put me to sleep either. Homework is just annoyingly difficult sometimes and involves formulas not used in class but easily found online.

Wish I could give zero stars, literally the worst professor I've ever had. He reads typed-out derivations directly from slides that he pretty clearly made like a decade ago. He mumbles a lot and is super hard to understand. I am completely self-teaching myself this class. Avoid taking him is you value your grade or sanity!!

BEST PROFESSOR!!! Gives so many extra credit opportunities. Though he seems strict because of mandatory attendance, he actually the nicest guy who genuinely cares about his students. Gives so much study material to prepare you for exam, the practice exams are identical to what will be on the exams.
Do not take him. No material, bad notes, no practice questions. Stat400 should not be as hard as he makes it.

I thought he was a good professor for STAT401. The class was weighted super heavily on exams (84% of our grade was determined by 3 exams). However, I thought the exams were fair for the most part, and the final wasn't cumulative which was nice. There was a super low workload in terms of homework and other stuff. There is a weekly homework with two problems on it. There was also a pretty easy coding assignment at the end of the semester. I thought the lectures were pretty informative and well-structured. Overall, I would definitely recommend taking Dr. Wellershoff for STAT 401.

Pros: 1) Very personable and clearly cares about the subject and his students 2) Will gladly answer questions both in class and during office hours 3) Held 3 office hours throughout the week 4) Exams were extremely fair, questions directly ripped from his study guide Cons: 1) Does not respond to email, essentially MIA outside of office hours and class (main reason he lost a star) 2) This was his first time teaching STAT410 so his notation was inconsistent at times and made the class slightly more confusing 3) Does not have the best intuitive explanation for some of the definitions and concepts, however this could both be just my limited exposure to statistics and the fact that he had taught this class for the first time 4) Homework was assigned on a chapter basis, not a weekly basis. Frequently assigned large homework sets that were due a week after being assigned. 5) Office hours were split with Math141 students Overall solid professor, but there are a few aspects of his teaching style I am not 100% comfortable with.

I've been on the fence between one and two stars for a while, but what pushed me over the edge was Professor Saegusa's inconsistent (and quite frankly, insensitive) homework spacing. Professor Saegusa is barely able to communicate any of the material, and when he does, it is often a proof irrelevant to the homework/tests or a theorem riddled with typos. Don't get me wrong, I like math, but I only want to see the underlying theorem if the professor is capable of communicating the material relevant to homework/tests in the remaining time, and he simply isn't. His tests frequently came with a massive time crunch that left the entire class scoring poorly. Despite this, he only curved one of our exams. I am not salty about a poor grade, in fact I am doing well. Rather, this fits into a constant pattern of him being insensitive about the time we need to do things, be it taking or scanning a test, or going from spacing his homeworks once every three weeks to once a week. That last thing really got on my nerves: his homeworks tend to take 5-10 hours, and there were a few weeks where I did not budget time for them, only to find out Tuesday that we had a homework due Friday. This was incredibly inconsiderate of our time; if you want to go from giving homework once every three weeks to once a week, the students need more of a heads up. He isn't necessarily mean, just inconsiderate. Essentially, if you decide to take Professor Saegusa, know that you will be teaching yourself much of the material, that he will assign homework inconsistently but frequently, that his tests are on a huge time crunch, and that his slides are riddled with typos. Do not recommend, though I know (sadly) that both of the STAT420 options aren't good ones.

This is for the Spring 2022 Semester despite the review date posted. Pros: Online Exams, Posts all slides, He doesn't believe in +/-, so it's A from 90-100, B, C, etc. , Cons: Online assignments due every week and homework, Gives a sample review guide for exams but no answer key (also will not go over the guide unless you ask him for the answer) When you ask a question about the content or don't know, he's the type of professor to respond with, "What do you think the answer is?" so if that makes you anxious, avoid him. He's a bit condescending when clarifying concepts as well. If you ask for clarifications for online assignments/projects, he responds with "read the directions." and that's it. The class itself isn't hard so I was able to get an A but I did not like the style of the professor.

i wish i could give zero stars. DO NOT TAKE RANKIN. please. you have been warned. i will try to sum everything up in bullets. in terms of the exams - exams are online on a lockdown browser - her exam style is that of upper level bio courses. - the format of questions is extremely confusing and often has many answer choices (two of the above, three of the above, all of the above, none of the above) for EVERY question. not one question is straight forward. It’s almost like she designs it for failure. - we did so bad on the first exam she had to give us a retake. - you have 45 minutes for about 40 questions. - the questions are extremely long. im talking a paragraph PER question. - almost all questions are conceptual applications and do not directly apply to what we learned in class AT ALL. - lots of math questions with no calculator! - zero practice problems to prepare for the exam. like none. - she makes these huge study guides that do not have any helpful content actually found on the exam - lots of material on the exam involved slides or IMAGES on slides that were completely skipped during lecture. - she will literally write the scientific name of a creature instead of the common name so you dont know what she’s talking about. brother i dont know the latin name for an earthworm STOP IT! - the exam averages are failing - no curves! she does award maybe 10 to 15 points of partial credit back though. - she does not accept criticism about the exam and will tell that to your face <3 in terms of the class itself - every lecture is just her reading off dense slides - many times, slides were not posted before lecture - the simbio tutorials are the “homework” and are extremely long. they take HOURS each, and multiple were due in one day. not to mention they did not help prepare us for the exam at all. she actually said verbatim that some of the simbio textbook was inaccurate. - the grade distribution on canvas was wrong the whole semester. we were unable to know our grades in the class for months. - we each paid about forty dollars for point solutions polling software. its like kahoot but graded and she never gives you the access code. many of us got zeroes in our grade book despite participating in all polls. when we asked her about it she said to “contact the point solutions company” because she didnt know what was wrong. - she provided no avenue to help us improve our grades despite very low exam averages. in short, she wants you to fail. i dont think she’s evil, i just think she is 1) over 80 years old and 2) just doesn’t know how to teach an intro level class. the TAs were extremely unhelpful as well. if you end up like me and dont catch on until its too late to drop, here’s my personal advice - dont just copy whats on the slides during class, unless that’s truly how you learn best. either sit and pay attention to what she’s saying or annotate the slides as she is talking. - do not spent too much time on the simbio assignments. they are essentially useless. i think only 1 question of all 3 exams was based on the simbio. - use the optional Hillis et. al textbook that she mentions in the syllabus. it is more helpful than the simbio at actually explaining difficult concepts - use flashcards to memorize definitions. there’s a lot of them. - ask ai or google to make conceptual applications and type k questions for the unit you are learning. - do not cram the night before! please. - dont beat yourself up about your grades. its truly not your fault. good luck and god speed. you should start praying from now.

161 is a very easy class. Almost painfully easy. Every lab is done online with Top Hat, which makes you wonder why the course is even taught in person. A lot of time is wasted waiting for the TA to explain things that we could easily figure out ourselves, or that we already learned about in lecture. For the most part, the instructions are clear, but not always. Two of the labs are group projects that have a bit more work involved, but the TAs are helpful letting you know everything you need to include. There's no final exam, but there is an individual final project where you just have to go out and watch birds for 10 minutes, three days in a row, and answer a bunch of questions. As long as you turn in everything on time, you're basically guaranteed an A.

Spring of 2025 was the test run for Dr. Buchner's first semester doing in person microbiology exams, and I think this contributed to why the exams were like /that/. I think Dr. Buchner does know a lot about microbiology, and he is clearly passionate about it. He was nice (at least in my experience, though I have heard from others getting not so nice emails) and some classes were funny. So for that, I will give 2 stars. But, he falls a bit flat when it comes to teaching. I have mixed feelings about the flipped lecture format, because there are some benefits and some downsides to it. However, my biggest gripes with this class was: 1. We were blind when it came to exams. There was 0 preparation when it came to the first exam, besides a heads up on the drawing, and the average was failing. There are no curves (not even a little) despite this. The second exam was prepared for us by some nice TAs. With the final, again, it was prepared for us by some nice TAs. I think the TAs did a lot of the heavy lifting. Props to them, but not to Buchner. I think I did okay on the final (at least above average, just estimating) but it was objectively bad. 2. Sometimes in lecture he went on to ramble about things that did not matter. Oh, and he added bonus content to the exam (stuff about HIV and COVID) which was not in the syllabus whatsoever and was only added because we happened to be a couple classes ahead of schedule. So, instead of using those classes to do a proper review, he just talked about the things he liked. I will admit I do find this stuff interesting, but I believe that being tested on it and wasting valuable class time on it is unfair. Unrelated to Dr Buchner: Lab definitely helped boost my grade. My lab group started off pretty iffy at the beginning and I felt like I was doing a lot of the heavy lifting, but halfway through they started doing more. So whatever. Genuinely a VERY GOOD teacher. Super knowledgeable and geeky. He goes over the essentials of what exactly you need to know for every exam, uses very neat concise slides with diagrams that aren't too confusing, and records his lectures. He also lets you make up any TopHat questions you missed as long as you let him know within a week of the missed day. The lectures are quick and boring (he Yaps with a capital Y), BUT the recordings make up for that since he explains the concepts incredibly well and in a way that doesn't seem entirely like jargon. My only complaint is that there is too much material assigned for one semester so it feels like he's rushing, our class had a handful of topics we never got to go over at the end but for the final he just drops whatever he doesn't get to. The guy spends way too much time going over TopHat answers My tips for this class: - Don't read the textbook, it's a waste of time (unless you really want to) - He reuses lecture quiz questions and they can be easily found - Use Anki flashcards for everything. Put the topics into groups of three, study one group for a couple of days then move onto the next - Go over the recordings, skip through TopHat stuff and go back if you ever feel like you're starting to doze off. Seriously he will TELL you outright what you need to write down - Ask ChatGPT to explain anything to you that needs more clarification - Don't BS the labs. TAs do not care if you did an experiment or calculation wrong as long as you TRY. They know when you're just using ChatGPT to do your lab reports for you

Gen Chem 1 is going to be a hard class for many because its chemistry, thats pretty much given. Dr. Stocker was pretty good with breaking down concepts into things that aren't chemistry related (like Legos) so students could understand them better, which def helped. However, occasionally, I felt like she skipped into things that I felt needed more background knowledge. This lab is rough, and your experience really depends on your TA. Fortunately, the class is curved based on how everyone else does, so I got an A+. If you're taking this class, I highly recommend double-checking your post-lab questions with others, and if you lose points for any reason, ALWAYS submit a regrade request—it literally saved my grade!

Now keep in mind, it's 216, so the class isn't already easy. Concepts are already harder than usual when compared to content from 131/132. So I wouldn't say it's really easy to get an A in 216 generally. Pros: - Teaches really well. Like really well. You will understand computer systems on a deeper level than any other professor teaching 216 in my opinion. - He loves teaching. That means he's not like one of those professors with really bad quality slides and unorganized course structure. The entire course is structured and organized really well under him, so you'll definitely enjoy 216 somewhat with him. - Pre-recorded lectures. That means no need to go to lecture and you should still do fine - Lots of extra credit opportunities. Basically go to his classes, participate, and get engagement points, which can help you get extra credits. Even by participating on Piazza by responding to other people's questions should give you engagement points as well. He also gives these weekly quizzes which is basically like a free grade to you since you get unlimited tries. - Open Notes exams. This is honestly the best part of the class. Take really good notes in my opinion, organize it all really well (I suggest using Obsidian notes since that's what I used to organize it all). This is also why his exams are generally harder than usual I believe. - No secret tests on projects. This is honestly the best part of the projects. It would be horrible if there were secret tests as it would take eons to debug them. Cons: - Hard projects. Yea I had trouble doing his projects at times since it's quite convoluted and wack and sometimes really long. Especially the Assembly project (all the best with that one). It's not bad as in impossible Yoon level bad, it's just quite challenging and you will be getting a lot of headaches by trying to figure out his projects, but they do generally help with understanding the material. - Hard exams. Compared to Nelson, Kauffman's exams are generally hard. So you will have to study and practice a lot for his exams, as well as his final. It's not like impossible hard, it's do able, but there aren't a lot of practice materials in my opinion so yeah you'll have to look at his recordings, projects, and other materials for practice and all. REMEMBER, study your projects really well, it's definitely almost always on all of his exams. Overall he's a great professor, but I suggest taking Nelson if you can (although he can have some cons too) as he provides more exam materials.

Fawzi is my favorite professor I’ve ever had so far at UMD, at least as it stands through my first year. I’m going to preface this review: I took MATH310, another proofs class in the math department, a semester before this class, and as a result, knew almost all the proofs content (about 2/3 of the course) beforehand except for modular arithmetic. I still went to his lectures though. Full breakdown below: Lectures: Fawzi is probably the best lecturer I’ve had at Maryland. I had a subpar professor for MATH310, and as a result, struggled with proofs worse than I had struggled with any math class in my life (as someone who considered myself a math person). I managed to salvage a 78% in the class, but I was for sure no expert in proofs before taking this class. Fawzi has a way of breaking down concepts in a very simple, easy to follow, and entertaining way that makes his lectures really easy to follow and understand. I feel like as a result of taking 250, I understand proofs way better than after MATH310. Exams: He did complain that he wrote exams that were consistently too easy and mentioned they were going to get harder, but they never got harder, so I’ll take it. His exams consistently have pretty high scores, take mostly lighter content from the lecture, and are basically what you expect from going to lecture. He can be somewhat nitpicky on proof structure, but there’s no math professor out there that DOESN’T nitpick proof structure. One thing I will say is he can sometimes grade things pretty harshly with regards to partial credit. Quizzes: The pop quizzes are the biggest issue with this class for me. They’re mainly a way of keeping people going to discussions, since any given discussion can have a quiz, so you have to go to all of them. All the quizzes are pretty straightforward, and you should normally score 20/20 on them if you’re keeping up with the material. Don’t be afraid to send a regrade request if your grade is messed up and you have an equivalent answer, but don’t send any begging for partial credit (the same applies to exams). He won’t budge on that. TL;DR: Fantastic lecturer, pretty simple exams, and nice person. Not a fan of pop quizzes in discussion go. I feel like if he recorded lecture and announced quizzes, he’d be rated much higher, but he is 100% worth taking for any CS class.

CMSC320 with Max Lectures are interesting to begin with, and Max makes them entertaining as well. Couldn't have asked for a better early morning lecture (9:30 AM). The exams he gives attempt to replicate this vibe. Projects/Homeworks are really open ended, and honestly fun, (nothing like the highly specific, constraint ridden, edge-case-hell classes like 216 and 330). You are given data, and basically a single page of instruction of what he wants you to report on. You're free to be as extra, creative, or barebones as you want (being extra and creative often gets extra credit) Overall a great change of pace from the rest of the CS meatgrinder classes and highly recommend

Jose's approach to compilers is great for several reasons: - Fantastic lecture notes. There's basically a small textbook's worth of compilers material available any time to understand the class concepts. - Detailed videos. Excellent in tandem with the notes. - In person lectures are informative. Jose makes us work through conceptual problems in class so we can understand them before diving into code. Really valuable. - Take home exams. You are given more than enough time to take them and you can access the detailed notes. - Straightforward projects. The coding projects are small in scope (you get a week or so to do each one), but really help you reinforce important compiler concepts. They're super fun and not too difficult. I took this course in Spring 2021 Pros: + The inclusion of three midterms and a final in this course means that, even if your group is not doing well, you still have chances to increase your individual grade + For each exam, Golub provides a list of relevant topics along with practice questions to help prepare + Golub himself is very knowledgable about HCI, and is more than happy to answer any question regarding it Cons: - The inclusion of three midterms and a final in this course means that this course is probably significantly more work than you are anticipating - The course is largely based off of a group project, so if you don't like your randomly assigned group, good luck lol - Lectures are largely pointless, technical concepts are not important until exam time - For the group project of designing an app, the help provided by Golub and the TAs is largely design based. If your team is having technical roadblocks, they are, frankly, of little help. - Especially if you're having technical issues, the timeframe to create the actual technical application can very much feel like not enough time

Not a hard class to take, but lectures are mostly a waste of time except for the 30 mins a week he spends on answering lab questions and giving tips. One downside, is he doesn't use ELMS at all, so you have to be checking Piazza or the class website for updates, which just add an extra layer to keeping up to date with tasks.

Laxman is a great professor. He is very knowledgeable about algorithms (particularly graph algorithms and parallel algorithms). In my opinion, the coding parts were more challenging than the written part in most cases. He ended up giving a lot of extensions this semester, but hopefully in the future he will do a better job making the assignments doable in two weeks and sticking to that deadline. The ones towards the middle of the course are the hardest, but just try all of the problems, go to office hours and don't worry about your grade. The grading scheme is super favorable, so just focus on learning. The mitderm was easy as well.

Do not take Gottesman for this class unless you want a semester of the teacher trying to prevent you from getting good scores on Homeworks and Exams. This guy is extremely against any computer science in his class and actually baits students to try and use Python on the Homework, only to tell them after the fact that it's really impossible to solve the problem with Python so they just get the question wrong.

Tries to act like he's professional, yet consistently posts sloppy autograders late. The goat. If you ever have an opportunity to take him as a prof take him. I once had an issue with grading and he fixed it immediately. He is phenomenal at lecturing, and he is very funny. Take him!!

Definitely a great choice for a professor. If you have the opportunity to take Mellet for any course, I would highly recommend it. I really liked BSCI410 with Dr. Wu! Study terms and techniques well since many are similar, and you can lose a lot of points if you don't know the subtle differences. Extra credit was super generous, especially for the final group project- an A is very attainable, but requires a lot of work.

I don't know why people are giving her low ratings because she genuinely made CHEM easy to understand. If anything I thought she was going slow for many parts because she wanted us to understand it. I will say that the cherry on top though was definitely discussions because we worked through problems together and if you had any questions, you'd ask her. She made things so straightforward and easy, especially for her exams, she would provide study guides with topics you'd need to know which made studying easier. Overall, I would take her again, she was an amazing professor.

The experience you will have on this course is dependent on your lab TA and how cool they are. Mine was super chill and honestly made the class feel not that stressful. The lab manual is written pretty decently and you can ask your TA for clarification if you get confused. Completing the experiment successfully is honestly not that big of a deal as you can just grab someone else's data. They are all honestly pretty easy, but Experiment 5 (Solubility) expects you to place hot test tubes into an ice bath without the glass exploding (some exploded). Lab reports take up a lot of time, but I would recommend doing as much of the post lab questions as you can before you even do the experiment if you have free time during the week. A lot of the questions don't even require the data and are just conceptual questions based on the experiment. It saves you time and also makes what you are doing in the lab make sense. The grading on the lab reports is fair and I only got something other than 95+% on 1 report out of 11. Sometimes lab reports get graded as 0 in canvas before the TA grades them, so you will be stuck with a low grade until the TA grades it. Before every lab you have to do a pre-lab quiz which locks after you take it, so you don't even know the grade you will get or what questions you got wrong until weeks after. They are pretty easy though. You also take post-lab quizzes which are sometimes vague and downright confusing. Expect to get 30-50% on at least 2 of them. I actually saw Dr. Guest because my TA slept in and missed our section. She was actually helpful and was understanding of our situation, and let us off with doing the lab through the lab videos. She also gave our section an extra 3 day extension to turn in the lab report which is why I'm giving her +1 star. What was confusing is what you learn in the lab is ahead of what you learn in CHEM131 lecture, so sometimes you learn concepts in lab first before lecture. Additionally, you have no idea what your final grade is until the end of the semester, and the curve is very weird. I don't know how helpful office hours are because I didn't go to them. Overall, its criminal that this class is only 1 credit and you will spend a lot of time on this class, but if you put in the effort you should get out with a pretty good grade.

Midterm exams and final were identical to the practice exams he posted. Practically no need to learn anything but the practice exams. Honestly an okay teacher to take as long as you know how to be successful and use the resources he gives you. I love Dr. Hirschauer with all my heart. I do think her curves aren't as high as other orgo profs but her grades are very fair and she provides tons of practice problems to help guide studying. She's so cool and deserves everything in this world

I might be a little biased since I had Koppel for lecture too, but here's my take. The lab experiments themselves were honestly enjoyable — a few even ended early which was nice. The pre-lab questions were super manageable (just written ones from the manual), which I preferred over Gen Chem’s in-lab quizzes. Now for the frustrating parts. We were almost two months in before anything was graded (at least in my section), and the first few lab reports got graded super harshly. Everyone panicked because we’d already turned in like 6 reports with zero feedback. My grade ended up recovering, but it was annoying. That’s when I started going to office hours, which really helped — especially for the PLQs. They’re super specific, and sometimes even the TAs didn’t know what the questions were asking. The TAQs though… brutal. We had like 4 or 5 of them — 10-minute in-lab quizzes a week or two after each experiment. Everyone I knew was getting like 3/20 or 7/20. No real way to study for them, so hopefully there’s a curve. The IR workshop was a good grade booster, and the lab practical was actually easy. Just wish we got more timely feedback and maybe a study guide for the TAQs. Also, I had an easier time with the PLQs because Koppel’s lectures matched the lab content. People with Dixon had it rough — they were doing substitution and elimination labs before learning that stuff in class. So if Koppel’s teaching again, I’d recommend taking her for lecture too to make lab less painful. My review for koppel as a lecturer is a 5/5, I'm rating the lab itself a 3/5 because it was just frustrating - but what can you even expect from a lab?

I would give him 6 stars for this review if I could!

Professor Zhao is a great choice for Calc III. As mentioned in other reviews, he does do a lot of his teaching straight from the textbook, but he explains the concepts much better than the textbook does, and usually reinforces concepts with an example or two. He's also clearly very passionate in what he teaches, which makes lectures very engaging. There are no mandatory homework assignments, but he does post recommended problems to work on to reinforce understanding, so I didn't feel like I was constantly drowning in work for this class, nor like I was falling behind. He does go through the material very fast--he posted a tentative outline scheduling which sections we'd do each day, then instantly blew through his original plan to speed through the material. This makes the last chapter (the most difficult section) a bit tricky to learn--you will definitely have to do a lot of practice on your own outside of class to understand--but it also meant that we finished all the content before Thanksgiving break, and spent the entire time between break and finals just reviewing, giving you ample time to work on the sections you had problems with. His handwriting is small, so sit as close to the chalkboard as you can, it will save your grade. Also, don't feel scared to ask questions during lecture--he answers every question, and answers them well. He doesn't exactly post practice exams, rather just a list of problems to look at in the textbook which cover all the topics that would be on the exam, but if you show up to review sessions, discussions, and lectures, and pay attention to the practice problems that are emphasized in those, then you can figure out which topics to prioritize the most for exams. His exams are definitely difficult--and be warned that his curve at the end of the course is incredibly useless--but if you put the work and do a bunch of practice problems then they're definitely doable. Overall: Great teacher, but his speed through the course is a double-edged sword. I definitely recommend him for 241!

Dr. Ebrahimian is a good, organized lecturer. He also very much enjoys the process of problem-solving, and he is willing to field any questions. His class is more engaging than most 403 courses in a few ways: 1.) It covers somewhat more material (e.g., Sylow theorems, solvability, group presentations, which are not generally covered); 2.) To that end, he sometimes left material out of lectures to notes; 3.) He has weekly quizzes. Beyond the usual benefits of attending class, he also tends to draw exam and quiz problems from examples seen in class once, or in the extra examples/problems in his notes, or from the homework. In some cases, this has a slight problem insofar as it can mean two students might have equal overall understanding of the material tested by a particular question, but one of them, say, looked to the examples in the notes and say nearly the same question worked out, so they can do it basically immediately, whereas the other has to struggle through it and so spend less time on other problems. Of course, this is always a factor, but it seems somewhat distinguished here, so being studious is especially good in this class! Overall, a great professor and an important, interesting class for mathematics majors. The difficulty is probably 5/5 for most students, but it is also rewarding. The structure is essentially traditional with lecture, weekly p-sets, weekly quizzes, two midterms, and one final. I believe two quizzes and p-sets are dropped, and your lowest exam grade can be supplanted by your final, but otherwise, little or no curving.

Very organized, especially for a first-time tenure-track professor. The lecture presentation was clear with strong emphasis on building intuition and guiding students through proofs. I think it works especially well for the many students in 410 who are new to proofs and have this as their first proof-based math class. The homeworks are quite constructive as well and not just busywork. The main crux of his class structure is that the exams (2 midterms + final) make up 80% of your grade. The exams are structured so that they are around 4 questions (we only had 5 questions on the final), but with 1-2 questions being very challenging. Exam averages were around the 70% mark for this reason. However, the grading on the exams is quite forgiving, and more importantly, the class is heavily curved from the start. An 85% is an A, an 80% is an A-, a 60-69 is C range, a 70-79 is B range, etc. If you put good effort in to learning how to engineer proofs, you will at worst get a credit-applicable passing grade and at best get a phenomenal grade. Lectures/Discussion: - Actually very solid lectures, can be boring at times but nothing to complain about. Gives a good fundamental understanding of data structures, and provides informative slides. - Discussions often teach new concepts that WILL BE TESTED, so it is a good idea to go. Also TAs' are very helpful Projects: - Projects often times are usually some sort of data structure clone with a couple of utility methods often attached with it [usually the best part]. - Projects are often good for understanding the inner working of certain data structures and are quite interesting in that aspect as well, especially the utility methods - However, projects (especially earlier imo) in my opinion do a mediocre job of helping students understand how to apply said data structures. One could learn fundamentally how a structure works in a project, but when tasked to code an algorithm in a scenario, may draw a blank. Its like if you were taught how to build a car, then asked to drive it. One can infer but not without application practice [Some other professors do puzzle/game style projects instead] Quiz: some challenging, some chill, but usually well timed. Do not slack off on them though, be mindful. Exams: - Exams are generally formatted with a decent number of questions involving theory, and 3-4 coding questions - The coding questions particularly test algorithm development rather than coding methods of a ds (understandably and arguably more interesting as well) - Difficulty wise, the coding questions aren't exactly, "beyond our ability". They are decently designed questions which definitely push our algorithm skills to the limit. However the topic of exams became a big issue due to 2 main factors -> Time, Resources: - Time: Exams were wildly crunch in time, to the point that they are unfair. On average for a person learning these structures and concepts newly, it should take around 20 minutes per algorithm give or take a few minutes depending on question variety. However we have on average 3 of these questions on an exam + theory (although that part is not too bad) on a 50 minute exam. This often leads to serious time crunches and not enough time for someone to solve the problem with a correct solution. Hence why the final seemed a lot easier pacing wise since we actually had the time needed. This is most probably the reason for all the low test scores, and its not something to look over. Personally time was the biggest issue here. - Resources: Past exams given do not reflect the current difficulty. Yes this is intentional as you have probably seen in other reviews, but do not take that lightly. I am not here to complain about that specifically though. I believe the main issue here is partly that but also the fact that we get very minimal practice on ALGORITHM DEVELOPMENT in this class. Our projects as mentioned above often task us with making methods of a DS, and only a couple Utils which is usually beyond the scope of our test (though those are decent). Aside from that there is no coursework that we have, no homework or anything of the sort to help us practice algorithm development. Highly reccomend students to do LeetCode or any other interview style questions for the data structures learned, as those are the kind of questions that will be on the test (difficulty may not match exactly but take all the practice you'll get). Arguably this will also greatly help refine fundamental skills for the future too. But in general there is a big lack of in class resources for this department. - Anyway do not take these lightly, they do require a lot of effort so be aware of that. TLDR: I think Pedram's a decent professor with good TAs, but the time crunch on his exams primarily on the coding questions and lack of algorithm practice can make the class an unnecessary struggle. If you are someone who already religiously does LeetCode or any kind of algorithm practice outside of class/willing to put in that often insane amount of effort to finesse the exams quickly, by all means take him. But if you are new to all of these concepts and want to understand without the tests completely destroying your grade, maybe think twice.

First, I'm just going to start by saying, for CMSC330, it really doesn't matter much who your professor is. The lecture quizzes, projects, discussion content, TAs, quizzes, and exam content are all exactly the same. The only difference between Cliff and Anwar's sections are which professor's lecture you can attend, but even then, you can just not go to lecture or go to the other professor's lecture (some people found that they didn't really like Cliff's lectures and attended Anwar's instead---the class is big enough that I don't think people would notice). Unlike CMSC351, the professor doesn't make that much of a difference for this class, so don't freak out too much. That being said, I do think Dr. Mamat has the better slides and also more experience in the field, so if you do have a choice, I would probably choose him. Here are my comments on the course in general (this applies for both Dr. Mamat and Cliff's sections): - All the class information is available here: https://bakalian.cs.umd.edu/330 - Literally 44% of your grade is free. Why do I say this? Projects make up 40% of your grade and you get around two weeks for each of them (give or take). You can ask questions, ask the TAs, look up documentation, submit as many times as you want, etc. within those two weeks. Each project took me between two and eight hours. There is literally no reason not to get 100% on every project as long as you don't procrastinate. The median on every project was between 97% to 100%. So again, there's literally no reason not to get 100% on every project, and they make up 40% of your grade. - 4% of your grade is lecture quizzes, which are completely open internet. You can run the code on your own machine, and the lowest couple of lecture quizzes get dropped. So between the lecture quizzes and the projects, 44% of your grade should be completely free (as long as you don't procrastinate). - The quiz medians were: Quiz 1: 14.5/20, Quiz 2: 15/20, Quiz 3: 17.25/20, Quiz 4: 16/20. You get access to all of the course's quizzes and solutions from previous semesters, which is helpful for studying. I honestly found the quizzes to be harder than the midterms. I will say, though, that I didn't do very well on the first two quizzes, but after that, I started buckling down and really studying and I got 100s on the last two quizzes. You'll be fine as long as you study and really understand the content. - 46% of your grade is two midterms and the final. The medians were: Midterm 1: 83, Midterm 2: 87.5, Final (with extra credit): 89.48. Just like the quizzes, you get access to every previous midterm and their answer key, and around ~85% of the content on these exams is the same every semester. They do change things up a bit sometimes (like I think we did more garbage collection than they did in previous semesters), but most of the exams cover very similar content to previous semesters, so it's really helpful to take previous exams for practice. And yes, there's extra credit too. - The discussions were fine. I didn't find them too helpful. There were good review questions, but they were all in a publicly-available GitHub repository that you could look at without going to discussion. Honestly, unless you're really confused about something, you can usually just look up your question online or on Piazza. There are a gazillion resources out there for Ocaml and Rust. For Cliff in particular, I thought his lectures are okay. He goes at a very manageable pace; definitely not fast by any means. He can get pretty theoretical sometimes. He answers questions well. TLDR; This is a fairly easy class as long as you don't procrastinate on your projects and do previous quizzes/exams as practice. I would recommend not starting the projects any later than the weekend before they're due. You could definitely knock them out over the weekend (if you don't mind working on the weekends). I thought the content was fairly interesting, although obviously that's extremely subjective and is up to how interested you are in this type of stuff. I would recommend taking Dr. Mamat but it really doesn't matter that much.

tl;dr: one of my favorite professors and courses, but it's hard AND time consuming for most. prepares you really well though. median scores: Groupwork: 95.63% Homework: 87.96% Quizzes: 66.26% Exam 1: 80.38% Exam 2: 63.00% Exam 3: 63.50% Final: 73.25% Grade Median: ~75.52% (aligns with PlanetTerp grade data) Lectures: Energetic professor with really engaging lectures. Pretty necessary unless you're going to office hours to make up for what you missed, since the textbook isn't enough to go straight into the homework. Structure is introducing the topic, giving you the important definitions, and then walking through as many examples as possible, step by step, until time runs out. The examples are usually proofs that are already in the textbook or going to be on the homework, but sometimes it's a really hard proof (that you'll never have to recreate or remember) that introduces the topic at a high level to you. Homework: A few questions are similar to the ones walked through in class, but it's never as easy as just switching up the numbers in your answer. For the rest, you need the notes and textbook with you. The questions scale up in difficulty and build off each other, so it's not like you have to stare blankly at a question until a full proof pops in your head. Grading is mostly off attempting/completing every question, with 3 of them randomly selected to get graded on accuracy. (you should be going to office hours at least once a week before the deadline to get your homework checked over) Quiz and exam questions are modified homework questions, or something close enough that doing the homework would prepare you to solve it within the time limit. It won't always be a graded question that's selected for exams, so you really have to complete and understand the entire HW to be prepared for them. Quizzes: 10 minutes long and happen the lecture after the homework was due (so 2 days). Structure is one definition and one proof or just one proof. Exams: A lot for 50 minutes, but still doable imo. The second you get stuck, you should probably move on to rack up as much partial credit. At the start of exam review days, Kate tells you the weight of each question, what section it covers, and its format -- true/false, working with definitions, or a full proof. Grading: Partial credit is big, if you couldn't get the algebra down or connect the dots on one last part, you'd still get like 70-80% of the points on that question. You lose a small number of points for not including minor justifications like "because f is a function" or "because f is continuous". It's necessary you include them/understand why, but a little annoying since those points can add up to like 3-5% on exams when you're stressed and pressed for time. Other: - one homework, one quiz, and one groupwork dropped - lectures recorded on request - spent 6-10 hours per week, peaking at the start of proofs (week 2) and again at the MATH410 content (the last third) - the final is cumulative but really just Exam 3.5 - if you took CMSC250, basic proofs, set theory and relations/functions are the main overlap, but i don't remember if 250 went as deep as this for relations and functions - hints to groupwork posted after they're due - there's a day-by-day "reading calendar" on canvas that suggests what sections of the textbook to read and what homework questions you should try to have completed i think the course being so dense means it sticks with you heavy, cause this was the final I studied for the least

Find a group of friends and work on it together, and go to office hours with a TA who seems the most competent. And hint hint, the homework get reused usually each semester. Overall I would recommend taking PHYS132 with Buehrle, seems like a pretty chill and nice guy.

Dr. Girvan is the undeniable GOAT of PHYS260. Course material is not fun but she does everything she can to help you succeed. Midway through the semester she took 10 minutes out of class to ask how everyone felt about the course and what she could do more of/less of, and she definitely adjusted her lectures based on those responses. She gives tons of review resources, even making entire slideshows of the most important content on the exams and what to expect/what not to expect. She is clearly passionate about the field and is extremely receptible to questions and concerns. This class definitely takes a lot of effort on the student's end though, so make sure you do every practice problem she does in lectures when reviewing as she often repeats questions on her exams. I would recommend taking notes from her posted slides before lecture so that you can pay more attention to what she says, as the course is quite fast-paced.

Anson himself is very kind, he seems like a lovely person. But his lectures were awful. I could never understand what he was trying to explain to us so I decided to self study instead of going to lecture which was the right decision for me. He is very smart but I just couldn't deal with his lectures. The work itself is difficult but not unreasonably so, and the textbook is very helpful. Overall the class was good, but just be prepared to be doing your own learning most of the time.

I dreaded going to this class, and it was four times a week so that's not great. The material was middle school level math, and maybe that explains why Professor Griffin treated us like middle schoolers. He is incredibly strict about attendance (you can't miss a class or be late even though it's a huge lecture hall), gave us assigned seating, scolded people for wearing hoodies, and forced us to follow along with the slides on our computer the entire time (he walked around the room and stopped class to call out everyone who wasn't doing it). He also wastes a remarkable amount of time going over the syllabus at the beginning of every class, going on tangents about attendance (even though the people who are missing class won't be in the room to hear it??), and just generally complaining. This course could be self-taught, and I basically did that since his lectures were too frustrating to pay attention to. The only reason I gave him 2 stars is because he provided practice problems and practice tests that were just like the real ones, so it was easy to get an A. He's also somehow very nice in office hours. I would recommend taking another professor and getting Professor Griffin's study guides from a friend, unless you want to be ripping your hair out every class.
Do not take him!!! His explains the material very poorly, assigns impossible homework, and refused to give textbook sections/problems for additional practice.

He doesn't explain the big topics very clearly sometimes, especially the derivations for type 2 errors. He wants to explain things intuitively, but sometimes, his explanations aren't very intuitive. And because of this, I don't have an as deep of an understanding on certain topics as I would like. I think the class could also benefit from more in-class concrete examples on how concepts are applied (we were taught concepts with no examples, which was very difficult for me), and it would also be helpful if he spent less time in the beginning of class reviewing what we did the prior class (it would occasionally take 18 minutes out of the 50 minute class). But some of the positives to his class are that he lets us have cheat sheets during exams which are extremely helpful because I think memorizing all the formulas is trivial, he records all of the lectures which is tremendously helpful, and Fernandes is also the nicest guy who genuinely cares that his students and he emphasizes prioritizing learning over grades. He also tells occasion stories that I find interesting and he also connects to you on a deeper human level occasionally when he talks about the privileges of education that we have and how we shouldn't take it for granted. I have a lot of respect for him as a person and as a teacher, but there are some aspects of the class that he could improve on while continuing to teach this class.

Amazing teacher, very generous with office hours, she encourages participation in class and exams are very similar to homework. it is a tough class but she does everything to make it approachable. Don't hesitate to go talk to her if you feel like you're lost. She posts her lecture notes and follows the book quite closely.

Was a fine lecturer, but STAT 420 is one those classes where it either clicked right away and you did really well, or it just never did and you'll end up doing consistently poorly despite spending hours and hours studying. Maybe I'm just salty because he mentioned at the beginning of class that he would curve all tests so that the average score was an 80, but didn't end up doing that (I would have gotten a C- if he had)

I took this class in Fall 2021 Pros: + Genuinely nice guy, really wants you to do your best. For example, on the final he will tell you exactly what each question will be on + Gives extra credit for participation + You can pretty easily convince him to push back some deadlines Cons: - Speeds through SAS examples in class, you essentially need to learn SAS on your own. All in all focuses way more on statistical theory rather than SAS code, and the class is worse off for it. The class becomes much harder than it needs to be - The class has no sense of organization. Kedem may go over a concept for the whole class period and then go "oh don't worry about that I'll never ask about that" at the end. It's unclear how important each concept is - There is no online presence for the class. No ELMS page, no gradescope, nothing. This means the only way to know what is on each HW assignment is to ask Kedem, but if you forget, good luck. Additionally, HW assignments had to be handed in MANUALLY, ON PAPER. This was EXTREMELY annoying to most of us who did not have a consistent printing situation - There is no consistency as to when HW assignments are due. Some are due in 2 weeks, others in 2 days, you never really know - He is not the best lecturer, a lot of the time it's very unclear what he's going over

Very sweet, cares about her students, but she doesn’t curve nor drop any exam grades. She also posts recorded lectures which are great to review before exams. I think her exams are fair and definitely go over what she talks about during lecture.

Dr. Keller's lectures are veryyyyy hard to stay focused during. They can be annoying and sometimes pointless to attend since he posts all the lectures and slides. The course started off fairly easy however progressively got more content-heavy. As someone who took AP Biology in high school and did well in class and on the exam, I started to struggle towards the end so I can't imagine the level of difficulty for those who did not. I recommend him though, as long as you put in the effort, you should do fine.
This lab is fairly easy, pre-labs, in-labs and sometimes post lab assignments. Its ran by the TA, so your experience will depend on your TA.

This course is very content heavy. Opoku is very nice and funny but can be hard to understand. She provides study guides for each exam. Exams are kind of hard because of the multiple choice and T/F so make sure you know your stuff.

AWESOME professor. She knows her stuff and is extremely passionate about A&P. She brings a lot of energy into her lectures and makes them engaging. There's a good amount of memorization but that's just the nature of the course. She makes all the material very understandable. I was dreading this course but she made me love it! Hands down the best professor I've had at UMD.

Teacher lowkey yaps a lot and her slides are 50-60 slides every lecture, giving you a minute to jot notes or else you’re screwed and left behind in the dust. Course is super unclear and has way too much content, making every test just confusing and you’ll end up studying everything BUT the stuff on the test. Karlton also just praises her colleagues too much and even puts their ideas on exams despite it not even being published. You’re basically tested on her friends lol. She’s a nice person but not a good teacher. Don’t take her if you can’t focus and lock in well. Most of the learning will be done outside of class.

This class is honestly a mess. His slides and lectures are super confusing. It’s really hard to tell what he actually wants us to know for the exams, and the tests end up being way harder than he makes them sound. If you can take another professor, do it.

Like everyone this semester has said, I would give zero stars if it was an option. The recorded lecture videos are outdated and do not explain the content well. In class time was wasted as the prof would ramble on about measles, vaccines and whatever he felt like tbh, instead of going over useful material. Half the clicker questions he just told us to figure out on our own. None of the lab/homework assignments supplemented the material we were actually tested on, not to mention they were sooo many of them. The average was horrible on the first exam (which he refused to even mention) but better on the second only because of the amazing TAs. The final was absolutely traumatizing. He was also not helpful when asking clarification questions, just gave some long winded response that didn't make sense. If I didn't have a great lab group and amazing TAs, I would've dropped this class. Please do yourself a favor and take it in the fall with Tran.

This is my least favorite TA I have ever taken. I don't say this to be mean, simply to be accurate. When we would ask him questions we only ever received half assed answers that never actually answered our questions. I learned nothing from this man, and he truly made that entire lab feel as though it was a massive waste of my time. Overall, I do not think this man should be allowed to be a TA. There is truly not a single compliment I can give this man as though I feel like he has done nothing that I have viewed in a positive light.
